newsitem.title: USA: Stocks tumble on last day of year.
newsitem.headline: Stocks tumble on last day of year.

text.p: Blue-chips stocks slumped on the last day of the year Tuesday, but still posted a second straight year of strong gains.
Bonds dropped on stronger-than-expected economic data, while the dollar fell against most major currencies.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 101.10 points to 6,448.27, leaving it up 26 percent for the year after a rise of 33.5 percent in 1995. Tuesday's decline was the Dow's biggest loss since it fell 161.05 points on July 15.
In the broader market, winners edged losers, 1,283 to 1,237, on moderate volume of 395.2 million shares.

Tuesday's drop put a small dent in the Dow's rise for 1996 but coupled with its 1995 performance, the Dow has climbed 68.2 percent over the last two years, a run the likes of which has been seen only twice before, in 1927-28 and 1954-55.
The market's gains in 1996 came despite widespread predictions that inflation or weak corporate earnings would rain on Wall Street's parade.

A big part of Tuesday's losses came in the last hour of trading, well after the bond market absorbed a body blow from a pair of reports that pointed to faster economic growth next year that might signal a pickup in inflation.
The government said sales of new homes jumped a stronger-than-expected 14.2 percent in November, the steepest rise in more than 3-1/2 years.

In addition, consumer confidence soared in December, jumping to a reading of 113.8 from 109.5 in November, the Conference Board said. The business research group said the sharp rise in confidence this year suggests demand will help pave the way for economic strength in early 1997.

The news sent the bellwether 30-year Treasury tumbling 1-9/32 to 99-4/32, a drop of $12.8125 on a $1,000 bond, pushing its yield up to 6.64 percent from 6.54 percent on Monday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
"During the entire rally this year, stocks have moved up in tandem with bonds," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "Today, the long bond got whacked."
Although the dollar declined, traders played down the importance of the drop, which came in very light volume.
Financial markets in the United States and Europe will reopen Thursday, and trading in Japan will resume Monday.

"You have to keep in mind, too, that liquidity is so thin that this move is exaggerated," said Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International. "But essentially it was the stocks and bonds that got things started."
The dollar had climbed to a fresh 45-month high of 116.40 Japanese yen in Europe before the surprisingly strong U.S. economic numbers hit the market.
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 116.08 yen Tuesday, down from 116.15 yen Monday.
The dollar fell sharply to 1.5400 German marks from 1.5550 marks. The dollar's decline against the German currency was exacerbated by the mark's gains against the yen, according to traders.
In commodity markets, oil prices surged as traders focused on cold weather in Europe and ignored the outlook for moderate temperatures in the Northeast.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil for January delivery led energy prices higher, surging 2.27 cents a gallon to close at 72.84 cents. January gasoline ended up 1.06 cents a gallon at 70.67 cents, while February crude rose 55 cents a barrel to end at $25.92.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 share index hit a record close of 4,118.5, up 2.8 points, its fifth new closing peak of the past month and giving a gain of 11.6 percent from the end of 1995. The Tokyo stock market was closed for a market holiday.
